This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 185 columns across 2 data files.
#### Issues Identified

7 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

live_data_statements: Participants provided electronic informed consent before accessing the survey.

Recruitment occurred in two phases: roughly one-third of respondents were reached through mailing lists and social media, while the remaining participants were later recruited through the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/).
Individuals recruited via Prolific received financial compensation at a rate of £9 per hour, adjusted to the actual survey duration.

Analyses were conducted using the R Statistical language (version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2025) on Windows 11 x64 (build 26200 Participants 366 participants filled the survey at least partially. 1 participant reported being under the age of legal consent (15) and was excluded. 52 participants were missing all responses to the B-MMR scale, efficacy items, and hope scale and were excluded.

Participants had 42 unique nationalities and resided in 38 unique countries. 197 were from developed countries (Europe, North America, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Israel), and 112 were from developing countries.

Third, the adapted measure of music-based mood regulation referred broadly to climate-related emotions, a category that spans diverse positive and negative states; however, we did not assess which specific emotions participants were regulating (e.g., anger, anxiety, worry, hope), nor did we capture contextual features of musical engagement (e.g., listening situations, genre, or mode of interaction).

text.text: Climate change is associated with a range of emotional responses, yet little is known about the role of music in regulating climate-related emotions and supporting adaptive psychological outcomes.

Because music is widely used to regulate emotions and can foster positive affect, emotional coping, and resilience, it may also help individuals maintain hope when confronting the challenges of climate change.
The present study examined whether music-based mood regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope, and whether this relationship is mediated by climate efficacy beliefs.
A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 310 adults.

Participants reported their use of music to regulate climaterelated emotions, climate efficacy beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, collective efficacy, and collective outcome expectancy), and hope.
Relationships among the variables were examined using correlation analyses and structural equation modeling.
Several musicbased regulation strategies, particularly solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival, were positively associated with hope.

Some regulation strategies were also positively associated with self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, and collective outcome expectancy, whereas no significant bivariate associations emerged with collective efficacy.
Structural equation modeling indicated a significant total indirect effect of music-based regulation on hope through climate efficacy beliefs.
However, only self-efficacy and collective efficacy emerged as significant mediators.
Outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy did not significantly mediate the association.
The direct association between music-based regulation and hope remained significant, indicating partial mediation.

These findings suggest that individuals who use music to regulate climate-related emotions report greater hope and that this association is partly explained by stronger perceptions of personal and collective capability.
Climate efficacy beliefs emerged as a small yet significant pathway linking music-based regulation and hope.
Music may therefore represent an accessible everyday resource that supports adaptive engagement with climate emotions and fosters hope in the context of climate change.

The climate crisis increasingly shapes the texture of our daily emotional life, functioning not only as an environmental emergency but also as a profound psychological context (Doherty & Clayton, 2011).
text.formatted: The climate crisis increasingly shapes the texture of our daily emotional life, functioning not only as an environmental emergency but also as a profound psychological context <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Doherty & Clayton, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: As people encounter rising temperatures, extreme weather events and ecological degradation, they also experience a growing set of climate emotions that reflect both personal concern and broader existential threat, including eco-anxiety, eco-grief or eco-guilt (Pihkala, 2022).
text.formatted: As people encounter rising temperatures, extreme weather events and ecological degradation, they also experience a growing set of climate emotions that reflect both personal concern and broader existential threat, including eco-anxiety, eco-grief or eco-guilt <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Pihkala, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While these emotions can be challenging, they may also motivate engagement with environmental issues and climate action (Ogunbode et al., 2022).
text.formatted: While these emotions can be challenging, they may also motivate engagement with environmental issues and climate action <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ogunbode et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: An important factor that may shape whether individuals remain constructively engaged is hope.

Hope is a multifaceted psychological construct frequently defined as a cognitivemotivational state comprising agency (goal-directed determination) and pathways (planning to meet goals) (Snyder et al., 1991).
text.formatted: Hope is a multifaceted psychological construct frequently defined as a cognitivemotivational state comprising agency (goal-directed determination) and pathways (planning to meet goals) <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Snyder et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Recently, hope has been proposed as an antidote for eco-emotions and earth-related mental challenges (Laranjeira et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recently, hope has been proposed as an antidote for eco-emotions and earth-related mental challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Laranjeira et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Since how we perceive the future can hugely affect how we feel in the present, decades of positive psychology research has shown substantial associations of hope with subjective, psychological and social wellbeing (Murphy, 2023).
text.formatted: Since how we perceive the future can hugely affect how we feel in the present, decades of positive psychology research has shown substantial associations of hope with subjective, psychological and social wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Murphy, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Within the broaden-and-build theory (Fredricksonhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?XzQQis 2001) , hope functions as a positive emotion that widens individuals' momentary perspectives and action repertoire, and supports the development of psychological resources to deal with stressful situations.

text.text: In the climate context, hope may therefore help individuals maintain resilience, cope with uncertainty, and sustain long-term engagement with climate action (Pihkala, 2018).
text.formatted: In the climate context, hope may therefore help individuals maintain resilience, cope with uncertainty, and sustain long-term engagement with climate action <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Pihkala, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Given the importance of hope for psychological adaptation and sustained engagement in the climate crisis, it becomes increasingly important to understand how people regulate their climate emotions in everyday life (Ortner et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Given the importance of hope for psychological adaptation and sustained engagement in the climate crisis, it becomes increasingly important to understand how people regulate their climate emotions in everyday life <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ortner et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Climate emotions often arise unpredictably (e.g., through news exposure, weather anomalies, conversations, or personal reflections) and their intensity can fluctuate across daily contexts (Alabak & Verduyn, 2025).
text.formatted: Climate emotions often arise unpredictably (e.g., through news exposure, weather anomalies, conversations, or personal reflections) and their intensity can fluctuate across daily contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alabak & Verduyn, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Without effective regulation, these emotions may accumulate and contribute to heightened distress, rumination, or paralysis; conversely, when individuals are able to process and integrate their feelings, they are more likely to sustain constructive engagement and maintain a sense of hope (Alabak & Verduyn, 2025; Ibrahim, 2024).

text.text: For instance, recent experimental work shows that specific emotion-regulation strategies used in response to climate information can meaningfully alter emotional outcomes, such as reducing negative affect or increasing hope, and, in some cases, shape intentions to engage in climate-mitigating actions (Armstrong et al., 2025).

text.text: Everyday regulatory practices therefore play a crucial role in determining whether climate emotions become overwhelming or instead support adaptive coping, resilience, and future-oriented motivation.
Listening to music is one of the most widely used tools for affect regulation in everyday life (van Goethem & Sloboda, 2011).
text.formatted: Listening to music is one of the most widely used tools for affect regulation in everyday life <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(van Goethem & Sloboda, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: People turn to music across a wide range of situations from managing daily stress to navigating complex emotional experiences, because it is easily accessible, socially embedded, and capable of eliciting rapid shifts in physiological arousal, mood, and meaning (Feneberg et al., 2025).
text.formatted: People turn to music across a wide range of situations from managing daily stress to navigating complex emotional experiences, because it is easily accessible, socially embedded, and capable of eliciting rapid shifts in physiological arousal, mood, and meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Feneberg et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Music thus offers both immediate emotional modulation and deeper opportunities for reflection, expression, and coping, making it a versatile resource for regulating affect in everyday contexts.

Established models of music-based mood regulation (Saarikallio, 2012) show that people draw on diverse strategies (entertainment, revival, strong sensation, diversion, discharge, mental work, and solace) to manage, express, or transform emotional states in daily life.
text.formatted: Established models of music-based mood regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Saarikallio, 2012)</ref> show that people draw on diverse strategies (entertainment, revival, strong sensation, diversion, discharge, mental work, and solace) to manage, express, or transform emotional states in daily life.

text.text: The accessawareness-agency (AAA) model (Saarikallio, 2019) conceptualizes this process as the interplay of embodied access to emotional experience, reflective awareness of that experience, and a resulting sense of agency in shaping one's affective state.
text.formatted: The accessawareness-agency (AAA) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Saarikallio, 2019)</ref> conceptualizes this process as the interplay of embodied access to emotional experience, reflective awareness of that experience, and a resulting sense of agency in shaping one's affective state.

text.text: These components are particularly relevant for climate emotions, which are often morally complex, ambiguous, and intense, making them likely candidates for regulation through music.

Through embodied access, music can help individuals contact and articulate difficult climate-related feelings; through reflective awareness, it can support meaning-making and emotional clarity; and through agency, it may foster a sense of empowerment in the face of climate threats.
These processes suggest that music may help individuals process, contain, or reframe climate-related emotions in ways that influence their broader psychological functioning.
Accordingly, music and arts-based practices have been highlighted as vital pathways for individuals to work through climate emotions, manage stress and foster hope and resilience (Ibrahim, 2024).
text.formatted: Accordingly, music and arts-based practices have been highlighted as vital pathways for individuals to work through climate emotions, manage stress and foster hope and resilience <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Ibrahim, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Music, with its unique ability to entrain physiological rhythms and evoke complex emotional responses, has emerged as a potent medium for fostering hope, especially within music therapy and music medicine research (Wilson, 2025).
text.formatted: Music, with its unique ability to entrain physiological rhythms and evoke complex emotional responses, has emerged as a potent medium for fostering hope, especially within music therapy and music medicine research <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Wilson, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: By providing a safe haven for emotional expression and playful creativity, music helps individuals reconnect with their empowered selves and envision a meaningful future (Bennett et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By providing a safe haven for emotional expression and playful creativity, music helps individuals reconnect with their empowered selves and envision a meaningful future <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bennett et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Particularly in mental health and psychiatric care as well as oncology and palliative care, music interventions have shown significant improvements in hope and happiness (Jethva et al., 2025; Silverman, 2016).
text.formatted: Particularly in mental health and psychiatric care as well as oncology and palliative care, music interventions have shown significant improvements in hope and happiness <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Jethva et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Silverman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the hope-enhancing potential of music is not limited to clinical populations, as music listening in experiments has been found to increase self-reported hope among healthy adults (Gupta & Gupta, 2016; Ziv et al., 2011).

text.text: However, how music-based regulation of climate emotions relates to hope in climate contexts has received no academic attention so far.
Moreover, the psychological mechanisms through which such regulation might exert its effects, including potential pathways such as cognitive processes, remain largely underexplored.

Building on Social Cognitive Theory (Bandurahttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?CPCT5T 1986) , climate-efficacy beliefs represent core cognitive appraisals that shape how individuals interpret and respond to the climate crisis (Koletsou & Mancy, 2011).

text.text: Self-efficacy and collective efficacy beliefs capture the extent to which individuals feel personally capable of contributing to climate solutions and perceive groups as capable of acting effectively (Choi & Hart, 2021).
text.formatted: Self-efficacy and collective efficacy beliefs capture the extent to which individuals feel personally capable of contributing to climate solutions and perceive groups as capable of acting effectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Choi & Hart, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In parallel, outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy beliefs reflect whether people expect their own actions and coordinated collective efforts to produce meaningful environmental outcomes (Choi & Hart, 2021).
text.formatted: In parallel, outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy beliefs reflect whether people expect their own actions and coordinated collective efforts to produce meaningful environmental outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Choi & Hart, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A large body of research shows that these beliefs reliably predict climate change attitudeshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?pVC2el mitigation intentions, climate policy support and pro-environmental behavior (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?pVC2el  Choi & Hart, 2021; Hanss et al., 2025; Hurst Loo & Walker, 2023) , suggesting that feeling capable of influencing outcomes is a central driver of environmental views and action.

text.text: Furthermore, studies of high school students have identified perceived personal competence and trust in collective action as key predictors of hope in the context of climate change (Li & Monroe, 2019).

text.text: Especially constructive hopehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?iJty6M rooted in meaning-making, trust and positive reappraisal instead of denial, appears to be particularly relevant for climate engagement (Ojala, 2012) , highlighting the importance of strategies that help individuals navigate and transform their emotional responses to climate change.

text.text: Efficacy and outcome expectancy beliefs have also been studied extensively in health and wellbeing research, showing substantial benefits for mental and physical health (Brown et al., 2014; Lo et al., 2023).

text.text: Given this central role of efficacy beliefs in shaping both environmental action and emotional functioning, it is plausible that they also serve as a mechanism linking music-based regulation of climate emotions to wellbeing.

Regulating emotions through music-whether by gaining emotional clarity, expressing difficult feelings, or shifting one's perspective-may help individuals move from overwhelm toward a more coherent sense of agency (Saarikallio et al., 2020).

text.text: Based on the access-awareness-agency model (Saarikalliohttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?cs7gx8 2019) , such regulatory experiences through music can support the formation of stronger efficacy beliefs by fostering feelings of capability and empowerment.

text.text: For example, recent research shows that identifying strongly as a music person affects mental health only indirectly, because it boosts a person's self-efficacy, which in turn supports better wellbeing (Koehler et al., 2026).

text.text: At the same time, music-based meaning-making (e.g., through climate-themed lyrics) or connection with others through music (e.g., engaging with activist artists) may enhance outcome expectancy beliefs, reinforcing the perception that individual and collective efforts can produce meaningful environmental change.
Music-based regulation may therefore influence wellbeing partly through its impact on these core cognitive appraisals.

The present study aims to examine whether music-based regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope in the climate crisis, and whether these associations operate through climate-efficacy beliefs.

Building on research showing that music is a powerful tool for affect regulation and that efficacy-related cognitions are central to emotional resilience and climate engagement, the study proposes that music-based regulation may shape how capable and effective individuals feel in responding to climate change.
These efficacy beliefs, in turn, are expected to influence whether people experience greater hope.
We formulated the following hypotheses: H1 (Hope): Higher levels of music-based regulation of climate emotions are associated with higher hope.

Higher levels of music-based regulation of climate emotions are associated with stronger climate-efficacy beliefs (self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, collective efficacy, collective outcome expectancy).
The associations between music-based regulation and higher hope are mediated by stronger climate-efficacy beliefs.
This cross-sectional study was carried out between May 2025 and January 2026 using an online questionnaire administered via REDCap, which required 15 minutes to complete.
Participants provided electronic informed consent before accessing the survey.

Recruitment occurred in two phases: roughly one-third of respondents were reached through mailing lists and social media, while the remaining participants were later recruited through the Prolific platform (https://www.prolific.com/).

text.formatted: Mood regulation of climate emotions involving music were measured with the Brief Music in Mood Regulation Scale (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?k30y3X">B-MMR; Saarikallio, 2012),</ref> which captures seven strategies people use music to influence their emotional state: Entertainment, Revival, Strong Sensation, Diversion, Discharge, Mental Work, and Solace.

text.text: For the purposes of this study, the instructions were adapted to the climate context by asking participants: "When thoughts or feelings about climate change or environmental crises arise, how do you use music to regulate your emotions?"
Participants indicated their agreement with 21 items on a 5-point scale (1 = strongly disagree,5 = strongly agree).

Illustrative items include: "Music helps me to understand different feelings in myself" (Mental Work), "When stressful thoughts keep going round and round in my head, I start to listen to music to get them off my mind" (Diversion), "When everything feels bad, music understands and comforts me" (Solace).
For the purpose of this study, the overall mean was calculated, with higher scores indicating higher use of music in regulation of climate emotions.

Hope was measured with the Adult Hope Scale (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?2ff7y7  Snyder et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?2ff7y7 1991) , which captures two components of hope: agency (goal-directed determination) and pathways (perceived ability to generate routes toward goals).

text.text: Respondents indicated their agreement with 12 statements on an 8-point scale from 1 (definitely false) to 8 (definitely true), with higher scores reflecting greater dispositional hope.
Climate efficacy beliefs were measured using four single-item indicators adapted from previous research on efficacy beliefs in the climate crisis (Choi & Hart, 2021; Gregersen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Climate efficacy beliefs were measured using four single-item indicators adapted from previous research on efficacy beliefs in the climate crisis <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Choi & Hart, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gregersen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Personal climate self-efficacy was assessed with the question: "How confident are you that you can implement measures to reduce or avoid the impacts of climate change?"
Personal outcome expectancy was measured by asking: "How likely is it that your own actions would help reduce climate change?"
Collective efficacy was captured with the item: "How likely is it that many people will take measures to try to reduce climate change?"
Finally, collective outcome expectancy was assessed by asking: "If large numbers of people implemented such measures, how likely is it that this would reduce climate change?".
Each item was rated on an 11-point scale (1 = not at all confident/likely,11 = extremely confident/likely).
To address the research questions, we first examined pairwise correlations between the music for mood regulation strategies and the outcome measures.
Subscale measures were computed as the mean of responses across the items in the sub-scales.
Due to the ordinal nature of the data, pairwise correlations were computed with Kendall's tau.
Multiple comparison corrections were performed with the Bonferroni method.

Their mean age was 36.4 years (SD = 12.4; range = 18-82).

Participants had 42 unique nationalities and resided in 38 unique countries. 197 were from developed countries (Europe, North America, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Israel), and 112 were from developing countries.

text.text: Some components of climate efficacy were correlated with some B-MMR strategies.
Specifically, self-efficacy was positively correlated with solace, diversion, and revival.
Personal outcome expectancy showed the same pattern and additionally a positive correlation with music mood regulation for mental work.
Collective outcome expectancy was correlated with strategies of solace, mental work, diversion, and strong sensation.
No strategies were correlated with collective efficacy.
Hope was significantly correlated with using B-MMR strategies of solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival.
When examining the hope subscales separately, agency showed a similar pattern of associations.
However, the correlation between agency and solace was not significant, whereas solace was significantly correlated with pathways.
Conversely, diversion was significantly correlated with agency but not with pathways.
We assessed the measurement models of each scale with confirmatory factor analyses.

All scales violated the assumption of multivariate normality as assessed with Mardia's test.
Given the ordinal structure of the data and the violation of the multivariate normality assumption, modeling was performed with robust estimators of weighted least squares mean variance (WLSMV).

Chi-square tests of measurement model fit were significant for every scale, but the chi-square test is known to be sensitive to sample sizes, therefore we also examined approximate scaled fit indices: the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) with 90% confidence interval, and the Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR).
Typical cutoff values for the fit indices are CFI and TLI >= 0.90, RMSEA <= 0.08, and SRMR <= 0.10.

text.text: We report scaled and robust measures of these fit indices for transparent reporting of the measurement model fits.
Fit interpretations are provided in terms of the scaled indices.

The B-MMR was fit with the original structure including the seven subscales each consisting of three items and a higher order general B-MMR structure, but showed inadequate fit and was re-specified to include residual covariance for two similar items on the discharge subscale which then showed adequate fit (see the supplementary material).

We evaluated the 2-factor and 1-factor measurement model of the Hope scale and while a latent variable likelihood ratio test indicated that the 2-factor model was a better fit than the 1-factor model, the approximate fit indices were similarly poor for both models, and we chose to use the 1-factor model for several reasons including theoretical justification of interest in a general hope latent variable, and because of the very high correlation between the factors of Agency and Pathways (.935) which makes them virtually indistinguishable.
The 1-factor model of Hope was re-specified to include residual covariance for two similar items which then showed improved fit (see the supplementary material).
Still, RMSEA was above typical recommendations (scaled RMSEA = 0.110, 95%-CI [0.087, 0.133]; robust RMSEA = 0.096, 95%-CI [0.077, 0.116]).
However, RMSEA is sensitive to small degrees of freedom (Kenny et al., 2015) so this measurement model of the Adult Hope Scale was still used in the full measurement model.

text.text: Note that this mediation cannot be used to make causal claims because data was collected cross-sectionally, and these results should be interpreted with that caveat.

Music for mood regulation of climate emotions had a significant indirect effect on Hope through self-efficacy (b = 0.049, 95% CI [0.001, 0.104]) and collective efficacy (b = 0.022, 95% CI [0.002, 0.052]), but not through outcome expectancy (b = 0.025, 95% CI [-0.021, 0.076]) or collective outcome expectancy (b = 0.009, 95% CI [-0.023, 0.042]).
The total indirect effect was significant (b = 0.105, 95% CI [0.059, 0.158]), and the direct effect remained significant (b = 0.230, 95% CI [0.130, 0.329]), indicating partial mediation.
The mediation through self-efficacy and collective efficacy should be interpreted cautiously because these standardized effects are very small.

The present study examined whether music-based regulation of climate emotions is associated with hope, and whether this association operates through climate efficacy beliefs.
Overall, the findings provide evidence that individuals who report greater use of music to regulate climate-related emotions also report higher levels of hope.
Furthermore, climate efficacy beliefs partly accounted for this association, although not all efficacy dimensions played an equally important role.

These findings suggest that music may support adaptive engagement with climate-related emotions in ways that extend beyond immediate emotional relief and may contribute to psychological resources associated with coping with environmental challenges.
Consistent with H1, music-based mood regulation of climate emotions was positively associated with hope.
At the bivariate level, several specific regulation strategies, particularly solace, diversion, strong sensation, and revival, showed positive associations with hope.

These findings align with broader literature demonstrating that music can facilitate emotional coping, provide comfort during challenging circumstances, and foster positive emotional experiences (Koehler et al., 2023; Saarikallio et al., 2020; Schäfer et al., 2013).
text.formatted: These findings align with broader literature demonstrating that music can facilitate emotional coping, provide comfort during challenging circumstances, and foster positive emotional experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Koehler et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Saarikallio et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Schäfer et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: While most previous work has examined music's role in regulating general emotions, the present findings suggest that similar processes may be relevant when individuals confront climate-related distress.
Music may help individuals tolerate difficult climate emotions without becoming overwhelmed by them, thereby creating psychological conditions that support the maintenance of hope (Ziv et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Music may help individuals tolerate difficult climate emotions without becoming overwhelmed by them, thereby creating psychological conditions that support the maintenance of hope <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Ziv et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the strategies associated with hope were those that involve seeking emotional comfort (solace), temporarily distancing oneself from distressing thoughts (diversion), restoring energy and vitality (revival), or intensifying meaningful emotional experiences (strong sensation).

This suggests that hope may be supported not only by reducing negative affect but also by providing diverse psychological resources that help individuals remain psychologically engaged in the climate crisis.

Regarding the relationships between musical regulation of climate emotions and climate efficacy beliefs (H2), our findings revealed that some music-based regulation strategies were positively associated with self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, and collective outcome expectancy, whereas no significant correlations emerged between regulation strategies and collective efficacy.

Consistent with previous research on different psychological functions of climate efficacy beliefs (Hamann et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?aezPNg 2024) , our findings also suggest that not all efficacy beliefs are equally connected to how people use music in the context of climate emotions.

text.text: The strongest pattern emerged for beliefs about one's own ability to respond effectively to climate change, whereas associations with beliefs about collective action were less consistent.

One interpretation is that music-based regulation primarily operates at the level of individual emotional experience and may therefore be more closely linked to perceptions of personal capability than to broader judgments about societal action.

Concerning the mediation hypothesis (H3), our results showed that the overall indirect effect of music-based regulation on hope through climate efficacy beliefs was significant, indicating that efficacy beliefs constitute one pathway connecting music-based regulation and hope.
However, only self-efficacy and collective efficacy emerged as significant mediators.
Outcome expectancy and collective outcome expectancy did not significantly mediate the relationship.
This differential pattern across efficacy beliefs may provide insight into the mechanisms through which music-based regulation is associated with hope.

According to social cognitive theory (Bandurahttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?CyyERQ 1986) , efficacy beliefs reflect perceptions of capability ("Can I/we do something?"), whereas outcome expectancies reflect beliefs about whether actions will be effective ("Will it make a difference?").

text.text: Researchers have argued that these constructs should be distinguished rather than treated as a single form of efficacy (Choi, 2026).
text.formatted: Researchers have argued that these constructs should be distinguished rather than treated as a single form of efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Choi, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Music may be particularly well suited to supporting feelings of agency and capability by helping individuals manage difficult climate emotions, sustain engagement with climate issues, and avoid becoming overwhelmed.
In contrast, music may have less influence on beliefs about the likely effectiveness of climate action, which may depend more heavily on perceptions of political, social, and environmental realities.

From this perspective, music-based regulation may promote hope primarily by strengthening people's sense that they can respond to the climate crisis, rather than by increasing confidence that climate actions will necessarily succeed.

Our findings are consistent with previous research positioning efficacy beliefs as central psychological resources for coping with environmental threats (Hurst Loo & Walker, 2023; Li & Monroe, 2019; Ojala, 2012).
text.formatted: Our findings are consistent with previous research positioning efficacy beliefs as central psychological resources for coping with environmental threats <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hurst Loo & Walker, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Li & Monroe, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Ojala, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The mediation through collective efficacy was somewhat unexpected given the absence of significant bivariate correlations between the individual mood-regulation strategies and collective efficacy.
One explanation is that collective efficacy may become relevant only when considering overall music-based mood regulation as a latent construct rather than individual strategies in isolation.

Structural equation modeling accounts for shared variance across indicators and corrects for measurement error, potentially revealing relationships that are not evident at the observed-variable level.
Further, the direct association between musical regulation and hope remained significant after accounting for all efficacy beliefs, indicating partial rather than full mediation.

Although the indirect effects were statistically significant, their magnitude was small, suggesting that efficacy beliefs explain only a limited portion of the association between music-based regulation and hope.
This suggests that music may foster hope through additional mechanisms beyond cognitive pathways such as climate efficacy beliefs.

text.text: Hope may therefore arise not only from cognitive beliefs about effectiveness and agency but also from experiential and emotional processes supported by musical engagement.
The present findings have several implications for research on climate emotions and psychological adaptation to climate change.

First, they extend the literature on music and emotion regulation into the context of climate-related distress, suggesting that music may function not only as a tool for managing difficult emotions but also as a resource for sustaining hope in the face of environmental change.

While climate emotion research has increasingly focused on identifying adaptive coping resources (Ágoston et al.https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?8CBMbu 2022; Crandon et al., 2024) , musical engagement has received relatively little attention despite being a highly accessible and widely used everyday practice.

text.text: Second, the findings suggest that music may contribute to climate adaptation primarily by supporting feelings of agency rather than shaping beliefs about the effectiveness of climate action.

By helping individuals regulate difficult climate emotions and remain engaged, music may support the psychological capacity to act and persist in the face of environmental crisis, which may be especially important when confronting a complex and often overwhelming issue such as climate change.

More broadly, the results corroborate previous theoretical research (Ibrahim, 2024) that cultural and emotional practices may play an important role in supporting psychological adaptation to climate change.

text.text: In addition to policyhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?v96x3i education, and communication interventions, everyday resources that are already embedded in daily life, such as music (Feneberg et al., 2025) , may help individuals remain emotionally engaged with climate challenges while maintaining a sense of hope and possibility for the future.

text.text: This study has several limitations.

First, its cross-sectional design prevents inferences about temporal ordering or causality, and future experimental or longitudinal work is needed to clarify directionality among music-based regulation of climate emotions, climate efficacy beliefs, and wellbeing.
Further, the observed indirect effects through self-efficacy and collective efficacy were statistically significant but small.
These findings suggest that efficacy beliefs explain only a modest proportion of the association between music-based regulation and hope.

Future research should therefore investigate additional mediating mechanisms, such as meaning-making, emotional resilience, social connectedness, identity processes, or climate-related collective action, that may more fully account for how musical engagement contributes to hope in the context of climate change.

Second, we did not control for potentially relevant third variables-such as personality traits, environmental activism, general music listening habits, or broader emotion-regulation tendencies-which may influence both music use and psychological outcomes.

Third, the adapted measure of music-based mood regulation referred broadly to climate-related emotions, a category that spans diverse positive and negative states; however, we did not assess which specific emotions participants were regulating (e.g., anger, anxiety, worry, hope), nor did we capture contextual features of musical engagement (e.g., listening situations, genre, or mode of interaction).
Future research could examine whether different forms of musical engagement are particularly effective for regulating specific climate emotions and fostering hope.

Fourth, although recruitment included multiple channels, the sample may not be fully representative of the broader population, and online survey participation may select for individuals with higher digital literacy or stronger interest in climate issues.
Finally, single-item indicators were used to assess efficacy beliefs; while common in this literature, they may offer less precision than multi-item scales.

Similarly, although the Adult Hope Scale was selected because of its extensive use and strong theoretical foundation, alternative instruments developed specifically for environmental or climate-related contexts may capture hope about the climate crisis more directly.

Future research could therefore benefit from employing multi-item measures of climate efficacy beliefs and comparing different conceptualizations of climate-related constructs to assess the robustness of the observed associations.
The present study provides initial evidence that music-based regulation of climate emotions is associated with greater hope in the face of the climate crisis.
Climate efficacy beliefs partially explained this relationship, particularly self-efficacy and collective efficacy, although most of the association remained direct.
These findings suggest that music may support not only the regulation of difficult climate emotions but also provide psychological resources that help individuals remain hopeful and engaged.

As societies seek effective ways to cope with the emotional consequences of climate change, everyday cultural practices such as music may represent an important and largely overlooked source of psychological adaptation.
